text: You're given an array of tokens in Reverse Polish Notation. Each token is an integer or one of plus, minus, times, or divide. Evaluate the expression and return the result.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — Reverse Polish Notation is postfix: an operator applies to the two operands that come right before it, so there are no parentheses and no precedence to resolve. Is that right?
Exactly. Division truncates toward zero, and tokens can be negative.
Good — negatives matter. A token like minus eleven is a number, not a minus operator. So my is-this-an-operator test has to look at the whole token, not just the first character.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to convert back to infix, or build an expression tree. But that reintroduces the very complexity postfix removes. This problem reminds me of the classic stack evaluation of postfix expressions — postfix is built for a stack. Numbers get pushed; an operator pops its two operands, which are always the top two, computes, and pushes the result back.

Here's the plan. One: keep one int stack and make a single pass. Two: a number gets pushed; an operator pops y, then pops x, and pushes x op y. Three: the answer is the single remaining element. One thing worth flagging — operand order. The stack is last in, first out, so the right operand y is popped first and the left operand x second, and I compute x op y. For plus and times the order doesn't matter, but for minus and divide, swapping them gives the wrong answer. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One int stack, one loop over the tokens. A number gets parsed with s-t-o-i and pushed. For an operator, I pop y first, then x, and push x op y through an if-else chain. At the end I return the top. One thing worth flagging — the test op dot find token equals n-pos checks whether the whole token is a substring of the string plus, minus, times, divide. Operators are single characters and match. Any number string, including minus eleven, does not, so negatives are correctly treated as numbers.

Let's dry-run two, one, plus, three, times. I expect nine. The row that matters is the plus: y is one, x is two, and I push three. Each operator collapses the top two numbers into one sub-result, which feeds the next operator, and times turns three and three into nine. Order wouldn't matter for plus, but for minus it would. Let's also test corner cases. A single number, forty-two, returns just forty-two. Three, minus four, plus: minus four is pushed as a number, giving minus one. And six divided by minus one hundred thirty-two truncates toward zero to zero, matching C plus plus integer division.

The time complexity is linear: each token is handled once. The space complexity is linear for the stack, which holds up to about half the tokens. Oh, one more thing — if intermediate products could overflow, I'd switch the stack and arithmetic to long long. Multiplication is the most likely to overflow.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed postfix as operands are always the top two, so one stack and one pass suffice. You were precise that the right operand is popped first, and that it matters for minus and divide. And you caught that negative tokens must be matched as whole strings, not by first character. Good work.
